explanation: Both check n even and first half == second half; A does it with a Python loop (lines grow linearly 152071 at size 1024), B does it with one slice comparison executed in C (always 3 lines). B's untraced time does grow (8e-6 to 4.3e-5) but because the line count is flat the fingerprint reported slope ~0 with time=None, so B was read as O(1).
fix: When traced line count is flat, still fit the untraced wall-time slope (with a baseline/overhead subtraction) so C-level slice/compare work is classed O(n).

explanation: Both are earliest-deadline-first greedy schedulers (A day-by-day, B exam-by-exam sorted by deadline). The A-ladder scales m (the exam count) to 131072 while n stays 100, violating m <= n and the guarantee that all exams fall on different days (the ladder just repeats the same 6 exams), so the programs run on infeasible garbage: A does O(n*m) work per scan, B hits early -1/quit paths and C-level list.insert/bisect costs, giving O(n) vs O(n log n) with different primitives (sort vs bisect).
fix: Make the scaler respect task constraints (m <= n, distinct exam days), e.g. scale n and generate valid instances, or validate ladder inputs against the statement and discard invalid rungs.

explanation: Both use the same prefix-balance counting f(m)-f(m+1). A allocates a fixed list of 400003 entries per call via a comprehension (about 800k traced lines) so constant overhead dominates and the line slope over sizes 1..16384 is 0.04 (O(1)), while B allocates 2n+1 entries and shows a clean slope ~1. A's time slope is only ignored because lines were available; the untraced times show A flattening then growing linearly at large n.
fix: Fit the slope on the incremental cost (subtract the smallest-size baseline or fit a + b*n^k) or use sizes large enough that the constant term is negligible, so fixed-size preallocation does not hide O(n).

explanation: Both brute-force all 101x101 centers and verify against every clue. A has an early return when only one clue has h != 0 (sizes 1-2, about 56-81 lines) and otherwise does the full grid search (122748 lines at size 4), so the jump between rungs gives a bogus exponential slope of 5.5 and A's trace stops at size 4; B has no such branch and is a clean O(n). The scaled inputs also violate the constraints (N up to 66666 > 100, repeated identical coordinates).
fix: Generate ladder inputs that stay on the same branch (and satisfy N <= 100 / distinct points) and fit slopes only over rungs where the executed path is stable, or drop rungs preceding a branch change.

explanation: A peels off a greedy non-decreasing chain per color and B does first-fit over colors by last character; both produce the identical coloring and are the same greedy algorithm, with cost O(n * colors) where colors <= 26 so both are effectively O(26n). The fingerprint (both O(n log n) with noisy slopes 1.5 and 1.28, nest2) correctly says same; the labeller's O(n*colors) vs first-fit complexity distinction is not real.

A looks up the first index of a value in an array (O(1)), B does `i in met[:-1]`, a slice copy plus linear scan in C (O(n) per element, O(n^2) total) with early exit. The natural ladder has many tiny tests (per-test n <= 29, tokens 5..167) and the quadratic work is hidden in C builtins, so traced lines look linear for both (slopes 0.86 and 0.90) and the time slope was not used (None).
fix: Detect C-level linear ops (in/slice on growing list) via a per-primitive 'list membership/slice' feature in L3, or use time slope on inputs with a single large test case (n up to 5000) rather than many small ones.

explanation: A runs a binary search (about 30 iterations) per query, B uses a closed-form division, a real algorithmic difference per query. The ladder scales only the number of queries q (copies of the same line, capped at 1e5 so the curve flattens after 4096), so both programs are linear in q and the log(k) factor per query is constant and invisible; the traces differ only by constant (about 1100 vs 150 lines at size 1).
fix: Add a ladder dimension that scales the magnitude of numeric values (k, n, a, b) alongside q so per-query loop counts like log(k) show up as growth, and avoid exceeding q's constraint cap.
